title: The Climate Fight: What Is the Hard Part?
body: There may be more than one road to the same goal, but the road taken must be neither so strict that states give up nor so loose that insufficient effort goes unpunished. The Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement were both ratified by many states to slow the warming of the planet by cutting greenhouse gas emissions. The Kyoto Protocol sought to back its targets with sanctions; the states that ratified the Paris Agreement set their targets freely, without fear of sanctions. Under Kyoto, only developed countries had committed to reducing greenhouse gas emissions. The United States, one of the biggest emitters, did not ratify the protocol, while countries classed as developing, such as China and India, were exempt from binding reduction targets. Canada, which had ratified it, became the first state to withdraw. Because it left before the end of the first period over which emissions were to be measured, it faced no sanctions. All the other states with targets met them on paper, but some got there by buying carbon credits. And because some major emitters, as developing countries, were under no obligation to set targets, the rise in emissions could not be slowed as much as intended. Under this protocol, the uneven sharing of the reduction burden and its high cost, together with the prospect of sanctions, daunted states. A state that could not meet its target on its own would either have to buy carbon credits or be held to a higher reduction target for the next period: punished, in other words, with more of the very thing it had already failed to do. The Paris Agreement, by contrast, set out from the start to encourage rather than punish: that was the price of keeping every party in the game. So, with no threat of sanctions, what would move states to act? One might expect a state's effort in this fight to grow in proportion to the cost of the disasters that climate change is likely to bring its way. Yet the overall trend can only be judged fairly if we bear in mind that not every country fighting emissions is a developed one, and that states struggling with more urgent needs are part of this effort too. Indeed, the Paris Agreement recognized from the outset that it would take longer for emissions in developing countries to stop rising and begin to fall. The largest sources of the greenhouse gas emissions that have been climbing since the Industrial Revolution lie in humanity's basic needs, such as energy production, industry, transportation, buildings, agriculture and land use. Knowing the sources also reveals the paths to follow in cutting emissions. But it does not guarantee that every step to be taken will be equally easy. In fact, states will pose distinct challenges because of their differing characteristics. The more widely an emission source is used, the harder it is to fight. The United Kingdom, for example, came through its tough test with coal by closing its last coal-fired power plant. Yet even though coal plants were far fewer than the vehicles in domestic transportation and the buildings that need heating, this test took decades. With the fight now set to concentrate on transportation and heating, the test of cutting emissions has become several notches harder at once. The difficulty may also lie in the size of the targets themselves. Australia, one of the countries that set an ambitious reduction target, has made progress with renewables in its electricity supply; still, it needs wide-ranging policies and plans to match the scale of its goals. But to take effect in time, such plans and policies need both swift procedures and public support for the changes they bring. Being exposed to the dangers of a climate crisis driven by greenhouse gases will not, by itself, bring the money and capacity the fight requires. The climate crisis, however, needs no visa to cross borders, and the crises that erupt in individual countries end up having global effects. Chile is one of the countries caught right in the middle of this predicament. Add the flood risk forecast along its central coast to the danger of high temperatures in its northern regions, and a bigger fight becomes unavoidable; Chile does have plans and legislation for this. But the fight against the climate crisis is also a fight against its allies, such as a lack of capacity and funding. Even strong economies, to say nothing of developing countries, find each financial step more exhausting than the last as they change their habits. On the other hand, not every drop in the statistics is necessarily a sign of success in the fight. Some statistics mask carbon leakage or the like. Japan, for instance, named the decarbonization of power generation and falling domestic output in manufacturing as the main reasons its emissions declined. But a decline in domestic manufacturing does not show that consumption of goods whose production generates emissions has fallen too. In cases like these, then, the emissions do not disappear; they merely move elsewhere and live on as a global burden. Like individuals, states sometimes seem willing and then back down along the way. If commitments are backed by sanctions, the loopholes in agreements must be closed so that no party can walk away without paying a price, as was possible under Kyoto. If they are not, it is probably wiser to build the main plan around how states have behaved in the past. Indeed, Canada, the first country to abandon the Kyoto Protocol, makes the point clearer: through regulations that halted the fuel charge, it has done away with mandatory carbon pricing for consumers. Clearly, the fight against emissions and the climate crisis is costly for states. Still, they may seem to have stayed in the game. So, as governments change and economic conditions bear down on them, will the sanction-free model of international agreements turn such agreements into group therapy? We do not know the answer yet, but unless carbon emissions are cut on a large scale, the world will keep warming. As storms grow fiercer, we may see a considerable rise in floods and in the number of species that disappear. Perhaps, a few decades from now, when scientists look back at the genetic maps of natural disasters, they will realize that the disasters yet to come because of the global climate crisis descend from the same lineage as the ones we have been living through for some time.

title: Why the same heat kills more in some places
dek: A heat wave is counted twice: by thermometers, and by the registers of deaths. Plans work on the gap between the two.
body: There are two ways to read the trace left by a heat wave: one is the relentless rise of mercury in the thermometer, the other the silent sorrow of death registers. In the shadow of the climate crisis, the fate of cities is determined by how prepared they are for the gap between these two realities. In August 2003, when Paris's famously romantic summer evenings gave way to a suffocating disaster, France recorded about 14,800 more deaths than expected in the first twenty days of the month. This was a surge of around 60 percent, and most of the victims were elderly people who breathed their last alone at home. The tragedy proved that public health is not merely a medical issue, but an administrative one. France woke from its slumber and drew up a national action plan: alerts issued by area, lists of isolated older people kept by town halls, and special instructions for care homes and hospitals. The city of Ahmedabad in western India learned the same lesson in the scorching May of 2010, when it buried 1,344 of its residents. Its response in 2013 was a heat action plan: early warnings, the mobilization of health workers, drinking water and shade in public places, and later a "cool roofs" program that lowers indoor temperatures in poor neighborhoods – an effort credited with preventing nearly 2,300 premature deaths. Japan, on the other hand, seeks its answer in technical precision, relying on a single number. When an index that melts heat, humidity and sunlight into one figure is forecast to reach 33, nationwide alerts go out; in 2024 a stronger alert was added for days when the index is forecast to reach 35 or above. There were 613 alerts in the first year and 1,722 in 2024. A study estimated that 61,672 people died from the heat across 35 European countries in the summer of 2022, with women dying at a markedly higher rate than men. That figure whispers how far an entire continent still lags in its test against nature.

title: Who keeps the clock?
dek: Most governments now agree the twice-yearly clock change has outlived its use. They disagree on which hour to keep.
body: Twice a year, in the dead of night, when we move our clocks an hour forward or back, we are not really playing with time but with an illusion of our own invention. Most governments now agree that this artificial pendulum swing has outlived its usefulness. But the real quarrel breaks out when the question is asked: "Which hour will we keep?" When the European Union put this rule, in place since 2001, to a public consultation in 2018, an overwhelming 84 percent of the 4.6 million respondents wanted the clock changes to stop. Although the European Parliament voted in 2019 to end the practice by 2021, the political chessboard among member states remains deadlocked. Imagine it: if one country chooses summer daylight and its neighbor opts for winter mornings, the two could end up an hour apart, and the map of Europe could turn into a patchwork of time zones. Russia acted as a laboratory for this dilemma. It moved the clocks forward in 2011 and left them there; but endless summer time did not last, and a law passed in July 2014 set the clocks back an hour for good, this time to permanent winter time. Across the ocean, the United States Senate passed the Sunshine Protection Act in 2022 to make summer time permanent, only for the bill to gather dust in the House of Representatives and lapse. The medical world raises a serious objection: the American Academy of Sleep Medicine argues for permanent standard time, which it says matches the body clock more closely, and points to more heart events and road accidents in the days after the spring change. Brazil and Mexico simply ended the practice: Brazil in 2019, after its energy ministry found it no longer saved much electricity, and Mexico in 2022, by a vote of its Senate. It seems that stopping the change is everyone's shared wish; deciding whether to bid farewell to dark winter mornings or long, golden summer evenings is where the roads part.

title: Does migration move voters to the right?
dek: Studies that follow where newcomers actually settled find an effect, but its size and even its direction depend on contact.
body: Migration routes do not just rewrite demographics; they change the chemistry of the ballot box. But exactly how? The question usually gets lost in the noise of political polling; we find the answer instead in those quiet, experimental periods when the state, not the migrants, decided where people would settle. Denmark's policy from 1986 to 1998 holds up a clear mirror. When refugees were placed in municipalities with little regard for local politics, studies found that in most municipalities, receiving more refugees raised support for anti-immigration parties. In the largest and most urban municipalities, however, the effect went the other way. A similar wind blew through Austria: where more immigrants lived, worries about jobs and about the quality of neighborhoods channeled votes to the far-right Freedom Party, especially when the newcomers had little formal education. The core of the issue, however, lies in the depth of contact. During the 2015 refugee movement, places where refugees merely passed through Austria – a brief, superficial exposure – saw support for the far right rise. But where asylum seekers stayed for months and became neighbors you might bump into at the grocery store, that support fell slightly. The Greek islands in 2015 confirm this: on shores suddenly reached by refugee boats, the far-right Golden Dawn gained about two percentage points more than on similar islands farther away. In short, migration's rightward pull is real but modest – a shift of a few points, not a landslide. Suddenness and unfamiliarity breed fear, whereas time, familiarity and sharing the same street can soften that sharp political edge. Most of this evidence, though, comes from Europe and from refugees rather than labor migrants, so it should travel to other places with care.

title: How many years does an earthquake cost an economy?
dek: For most countries, national output recovers within a few years. The places hit hardest can carry the loss for decades.
body: The bill for an earthquake isn't settled when the images of rubble fade from television screens; on the contrary, the real damage in the economy's capillaries begins that very day. The cost of collapsed bridges, pulverized factories and ruined ports – what we call "damage" – is merely the disaster's first face, counted only once. What remains invisible, stretching painfully over time, is the "loss of output": the value that city would have created over the years had it remained standing. Viewed from a distance, national economies are surprisingly resilient. Studies show that, on average, even very large disasters do not leave a lasting mark on national output, unless they are followed by radical political change such as a revolution. National averages, however, are masters at masking quiet, local tragedies. The January 1995 earthquake that struck Kobe, the pride of Japan, didn't just claim more than 6,400 lives; it wrecked much of what was then one of the world's busiest container ports. While the Japanese economy as a whole absorbed the shock, twenty years later Kobe's income per person was still markedly below its expected path, and the cargo its port lost to regional rivals never returned. The real tragedy lies in the scale of the disaster relative to the country's economy. When the 2010 earthquake shattered Haiti, the official assessment put damage and losses at around $7.8 billion – roughly 120 percent of the entire nation's output in the previous year. A shock of this magnitude cannot simply be patched up with insurance policies, reserve funds or a quick wave of reconstruction; it dictates the starting line for the nation's next decade. Ultimately, how many years an earthquake costs an economy is decided less by the fault lines than by choices made long before the ground moves: how much of the economy sits in the danger zone, whether buildings meet the code, whether businesses are insured, and how quickly reconstruction money arrives.

title: Bread on the table, and diabetes
dek: What the grain has kept matters more than whether bread is eaten at all.
body: When it comes to bread on the table, what the grain has kept matters more than whether bread is eaten at all. The WHO notes that adults living with diabetes rose from about 200 million in 1990 to about 830 million in 2022; most have type 2 diabetes, closely linked to excess weight and low activity. Research separates whole grain, which keeps the bran and the germ, from refined grain, which is mostly starch. People eating about three servings of whole grains a day had roughly a third lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes than those eating almost none, while refined grains showed no such association. Analyses following nearly 195,000 adults for decades reached similar results for whole-grain foods like dark bread, oatmeal and cereals. The usual explanation lies in fiber and structure: starch from white flour raises blood sugar fast, while bran slows digestion and prolongs fullness. These studies observe what people eat rather than assign it, and people who choose whole grains may differ in other ways. A brown color, too, is not proof of whole grain, which makes label-reading essential.

title: Does consuming more mean living better?
dek: Income and life satisfaction rise together, but each step buys less than the one before. The argument is over where, and for whom, it stops.
body: Does consuming more equate to living better? In 1974, Richard Easterlin noted a puzzle: within a country, richer people were happier, yet average happiness barely moved as countries grew wealthier – and a long argument about the meaning of growth began. However, research based on far larger surveys argues that doubling an income brings a similar gain whether one starts poor or rich, meaning each additional dollar buys less happiness. Do the gains ever stop? A study based on about 450,000 survey responses from American residents found that while overall life evaluation rose with income, day-to-day emotional improvement plateaued at about 75,000 dollars a year. In 2023, the two sides of the debate analyzed the data together and found that for most people, happiness keeps rising with income; the plateau applies only to the least happy fifth of people, beyond about 100,000 dollars. Furthermore, how money is spent matters: people spending money on others, as gifts or donations, reported greater happiness than those spending it on themselves.

title: How is sea level measured?
dek: A rise of a few millimeters a year is built from tide gauges, satellites and a correction for land that moves.
body: The sea is never still; tides and winds move its surface daily. The oldest tool, the tide gauge, records water height against land, with the Permanent Service for Mean Sea Level collecting such records since 1933. Yet land moves too, with coastal cities often sinking as groundwater is pumped out, so modern gauges are paired with satellite positioning receivers that measure the movement of the land itself. Since 1992, satellites using radar altimeters have also measured the open ocean directly by timing radar pulses. Combined, these records reveal a stark truth: according to the IPCC, global mean sea level rose by about 20 centimeters between 1901 and 2018, with the rate accelerating from 1.9 millimeters a year (1971-2006) to 3.7 millimeters (2006-2018). As warming water expands and melting glaciers add water to the oceans, the fate of coasts is dictated by this relentless, millimeter-by-millimeter advance.

title: Why are rivers running dry?
dek: Some of the world's great rivers no longer reach the sea for part of the year. The main cause lies upstream, in fields and reservoirs.
body: Some of the world's most magnificent rivers no longer reach the sea. Because its water is divided among seven US states and Mexico and nearly all of it is taken for farms and cities, the Colorado River has failed to reach the sea for most years since the 1960s. Similarly, massive diversions of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers for cotton irrigation shrank the once-mighty Aral Sea to a mere fraction of its size. The true culprit is human choice rather than nature. According to the FAO, agriculture accounts for about 70 percent of fresh water taken globally. Furthermore, a global mapping found that only 37 percent of rivers longer than 1,000 kilometers still flow freely along their whole length. While a warming climate makes the problem worse, these rivers often run dry not from a lack of rainfall, but because of decisions made on paper about how much water to take.

title: How do city lights affect sleep?
dek: Most people now live under a night sky that never fully darkens. The body's clock reads that light as a signal.
body: Most people now try to sleep under a sky that never truly darkens and whose stars are fading. A 2016 mapping found that over 80 percent of the world's population – and over 99 percent in the US and Europe – live under light-polluted skies, hiding the Milky Way from a third of humanity. From volunteers' reports between 2011 and 2022, Kyba and colleagues calculated that the sky is brightening by about 9.6 percent a year. Our bodies read light as a "time signal." Evening light, especially blue light, delays the release of melatonin, the hormone preparing us for sleep, and the white LEDs now common in street lighting emit a large share of their light in that blue range. A study of nearly 16,000 Americans found that people in brighter areas tended to go to bed later, sleep less, and feel less satisfied with their rest. The link is an association, not proof; the light that reaches a bedroom also depends on curtains and screens. Cities that want darker nights have simple tools: downward-pointing shielded lamps, warmer hues, and dimming in the late hours.

title: How much water do data centers use?
dek: The answer has two parts: the water evaporated to cool the servers, and the water used to make their electricity.
body: The digital world and artificial intelligence possess an invisible thirst. Data centers are massive electricity users; the IEA estimates they consumed about 415 terawatt-hours in 2024 (1.5 percent of global electricity), a figure expected to more than double by 2030 as AI grows. In many large facilities, the immense heat from this electricity is removed by evaporating water in cooling towers, and that evaporated water never returns to the pipe. When the water used by thermal power plants to generate that electricity is added, the toll grows heavier. Researchers estimated that training the GPT-3 model in Microsoft's American data centers could have evaporated about 700,000 liters of clean fresh water on site alone. With every answer AI generates, it takes a sip of water from nature.

title: Which languages keep the record
dek: A public figure can be careful and still stop at the border of the language it was released in.
body: An official document released by the state is only as public as the borders of its language. From school guidance to census notes, any record published in a language not spoken in a city's homes is formally public but practically closed. UNESCO highlights this gap by noting that a large share of learners are not taught in a language they understand well. Statistical databases suffer from the same bottleneck; for instance, while the UN Sustainable Development Goals database tries to keep indicators in more than one UN language, the depth of translation remains uneven. The true width of a public claim is measured by the number of languages in which it can be opened and read.

title: After ten million
dek: A megacity used to be an exception. The public record now has enough of them to compare the planning, not the skyline.
body: Once, "megacities" with populations over ten million were rare exceptions on the map; today, according to UN data, they form a class large enough to be compared with one another. Yet looking at glittering skylines or population tables tells us nothing about how those residents are actually housed. Data from institutions like the World Bank show how far official figures can disagree on informal settlements; a city may officially boom while the count of homes with actual services barely moves. What truly differentiates megacities is not the height of their towers, but whether their census and utility planning can keep pace with the people they encompass.

title: How grain actually moves
dek: Wheat, maize, and rice cross borders as balance sheets before they cross them as ships.
body: Long before wheat, maize, and rice cross oceans in ships, they cross borders as contracts and balance sheets in offices. Balance sheets published by agencies like the FAO (detailing production, trade and year-end stocks) reveal how concentrated the grain trade is. A small group of exporters still supplies a large share of traded wheat, and as AMIS data show, when a trade corridor slows, the paper trail makes clear which importing country will see the delay become a domestic question. However, reading these balance sheets accurately means noticing the gaps: sacks that never reach customs, cargo refused for quality, or harvest lost before the farm gate never make it into the official record.

title: The register of trials
dek: A study that never enters a public register is harder to find, and harder to count.
body: In the medical world, a clinical trial is a plan long before it is a result. Such plans – detailing who is enrolled and what is measured – can be filed in public registries before the first participant is even seen, and the WHO maintains a portal that searches all the registries meeting its standard in one place. The massive registry run by the US National Library of Medicine is the largest of these, but it is just one book, not the entire shelf. Medical journal editors treat trial registration not merely as a courtesy, but as a foundational piece of the scientific record. A trial that is never recorded in a public register, where one cannot walk back to see what initial question was asked, is far more likely to vanish in the dark.

title: The water cycle
dek: How the same water keeps moving between the sea, the sky and the land.
body: Water never stays in one place. The same water moves, again and again, between the sea, the sky and the land. This journey is called the water cycle. It begins with the sun. Heat from the sun warms the surface of the sea, and some of the water turns into an invisible gas: water vapor. Plants give off water vapor from their leaves, too. Warm, moist air rises. As it rises, it cools, and the vapor turns back into tiny droplets of water. Countless droplets together make a cloud. Inside the cloud, the droplets join and grow. When they become too heavy to float, they fall as rain, or as snow where the air is cold. On land, some of the water runs into streams and rivers. Some soaks into the ground and is stored there. Sooner or later, most of it reaches the sea again. And there, the sun warms it once more. The cycle never stops.
